1–9 
General Ledger Updates for Retail Banking 
Transactions 
Retail banking general ledger account transactions do not post via the accounting models. The 
postings that are made depend on rules specified for a product on the Product Transaction Types 
(PTTRM) screen. Two accounts are specified for every transaction that is permitted for a product: 
one for the product itself and one for the transaction.  
The Product Transaction Types (PTTRM) screen can pick up defaults for both general ledger 
accounts. The default general ledger account for a transaction code is defined on the Retail 
Transaction Definition (TRDFM) screen. The default for a product is defined with the product 
details on the Product Maintenance Screen 1 (PTA1M) for retail banking client accounts and on 
the Loan Product Maintenance - 2 (PTL2M) screen for retail loan accounts. The Product 
Maintenance screens are described in the Retail Clients and Accounts Administration Guide, the 
Retail Transaction Definition (TRDFM) screen is described in the Financial Transactions 
Reference Guide and the Loan Product Maintenance -2 (PTL2M) screen is described in the Retail 
Lending Administration Guide.  
The provision of two general ledger accounts for every combination of product and transaction 
enables you to group activity by product and by transaction. Therefore, on the transaction side you 
could group all proceeds from one type of transaction together (for example, deposits) or you 
could subdivide them into any size of group down to a single transaction code and product 
combination (for example, interest settlement on a savings account could update a different 
general ledger account to interest settlement on a current account). 
When a transaction occurs that causes the balance of a client account to be updated, there must be 
corresponding updates to the general ledger for the product. This occurs in the form of two 
postings: a debit and a credit. One posting is to the general ledger account for the product and the 
other to the general ledger account for the transaction (the transaction type determines which 
account receives the credit and which receives the debit). 
For example, the system generates three postings for a cash deposit of £100 to a current account: 
• 
Client’s account is credited with £100 
• 
Product general ledger account that represents the current account product is credited with 
£100 
• 
Transaction general ledger account that represents the cash till is debited with £100 
The following cases are handled slightly differently to the scenario outlined above: 
• 
Transactions that involve nostro accounts 
• 
Cross currency transactions 
• 
Credit interest accrual and settlement 
• 
Debit interest accrual and settlement 
• 
Deferred charges accrual and settlement 
• 
Loan account interest accrual and settlement 
• 
Loan account interest accrual and settlement on non-performing loans 
The above cases are explained below.
General Ledger Accounting Introduction 
1–10 
 
3937 0457-104 
Nostro Accounts 
In this case, there are three postings as usual: one to the client account that is the object of the 
transaction, one to the product general ledger account and one to the transaction general ledger 
account. The difference is that the transaction general ledger account cannot be determined until 
the currency and nostro number used by a transaction are known; these are included as part of the 
transaction details. The system can then access the nostro record indicated to determine the 
general ledger account and nostro to be updated. 
Cross Currency Transactions 
As it is important to retain control of the foreign currency exposure of a financial institution, an 
‘Other Currencies Control Account’ is held by the system in all currencies for each accounting 
centre. This enables the system to balance a multi-currency general ledger. This Other Currencies 
Control Account is specified as system wide parameter (see the description of the System 
Parameters (SPMTR) screen in the Guide to Setting Up the Retail System) and can be picked up 
by the system as the default transaction general ledger account when indicated for cross currency 
transactions. 
An example of a cross currency transaction is given below: 
Client Account A is a GBP account, transferring 100 GBP to Client Account B, which is a USD 
account. Assume that the exchange rate is 1 GBP to 1.5 USD. 
The postings created for the above transaction are: 
• 
Client Account A is debited with 100 GBP 
• 
Client Account B is credited with 150 USD 
• 
Product general ledger account that represents Client Account A's product is debited with 100 
GBP 
• 
Currency Control Account is credited with 100 GBP 
• 
Product general ledger account that represents Client Account B's product is debited with 150 
USD 
• 
Currency Control Account is debited with 150 USD 
Credit Interest Accrual and Settlement 
Credit interest is accrued in a separate product general ledger account where it remains until 
settlement. The balance of this account represents a liability and can be grouped by product or 
type of product. The transaction general ledger account represents the account in which such 
expenses are accumulated. 
When interest is settled, three postings are made: a credit to the client account that receives the 
interest, a debit from the product general ledger account where interest has accrued and a credit to 
the product general ledger account that represents the product balances.
General Ledger Accounting Introduction 
3937 0457-104 
 
1–11 
Debit Interest Accrual and Settlement 
Debit interest is accrued in a separate product general ledger account where it remains until 
settlement. The balance of this account represents an asset. The transaction general ledger account 
represents the account that receives such income. 
When interest is settled, three postings are made: a debit to the client account that pays the 
interest, a debit from the product general ledger account and a credit to the transaction general 
ledger account in which the interest for the product has accrued. 
Deferred Charges Accrual and Settlement 
Deferred charges are accrued in a product general ledger account where they remain until 
settlement. The balance of this account represents an asset. The transaction general ledger account 
represents the account that receives income from charges. 
When a deferred charge is settled, three postings are made: a debit to the client account that pays 
the charge, a debit from the product general ledger account where charge has been deferred and a 
credit to the transaction general ledger account in which income accumulates. 
Loan Account Interest Accrual and Settlement 
Interest accrual on a loan is represented by three transactions:  
• 
Loan interest accrual (transaction code 850) 
• 
Loan interest arrears interest accrual (transaction code 851) 
• 
Loan principal arrears interest accrual (transaction code 852) 
This gives you the opportunity to accrue the different types of interest in different product general 
ledger accounts so that they can be recorded as separate assets. At the same time, you use one 
transaction general ledger account to record income for the product. 
When interest is settled, the product general ledger account(s) where interest accrued is credited, 
the transaction general ledger account in which income accumulates is credited and the loan 
account itself is debited. 
Loan Account Interest Accrual and Settlement on Non-Performing Loans 
The same principal applies to interest on non-performing loans as to interest on performing loans 
in that the three types of interest can be accrued in separate general ledger accounts, the difference 
is that the general ledger account(s) are normally memo suspense general ledger accounts. This 
means that arrears accrual balances for non-performing loans are not reflected as income in your 
profit and loss statement and are not included as assets on your balance sheet.
General Ledger Accounting Introduction 
1–12 
 
3937 0457-104 
Event Charges 
Event charges are attached to events rather than financial transactions, for example providing a 
replacement statement. Event charge transactions are treated in the same way as ordinary 
withdrawal transactions. When an event charge is applied, the system makes three postings: the 
client’s account is debited, the product general ledger account for the client account is debited and 
the transaction general ledger account is credited. You could define a series of charge transaction 
general ledger accounts to separate different types of charge within the income area of the general 
ledger. 
Retail Cross Accounting Centre Postings 
If a transaction performed at one accounting centre is actioned against a real account held at 
another accounting centre, then cross accounting centre postings are required to balance the 
general ledger at each accounting centre. 
For example, the following postings are required for a cash deposit of £100 made at one 
accounting centre for a current account held at another accounting centre: 
• 
Client’s account is credited with £100 
• 
Product general ledger account that represents the current account product is credited with 
£100 at the accounting centre of the current account 
• 
Transaction general ledger account that represents the cash till is debited with £100 at the 
accounting centre where the transaction took place 
 
To enable the general ledger of each accounting centre to balance, the following additional 
postings are generated by the system: 
• 
At the accounting centre holding the client’s account, the general ledger account that 
represents cross accounting centre debits is debited with £100 
• 
At the accounting centre at which the transaction took place, the general ledger account that 
represents cross accounting centre credits is credited with £100 
 
The general ledger accounts to be used for the credits and debits between specified accounting 
centres can be defined using the Cross Accounting Centre Rules (ACRLM) screen, described in 
the Guide to Setting Up the Retail System.

Statutory Reporting 
The system provides an interface to rFRAME, the statutory reporting package from CMG. 
Information is extracted from the system and placed in flat files. These flat files are fed through to 
the rFRAME software that produces and sends the statutory reports. At present only Capital 
Adequacy Reports for the Bank of England are supported. 
The extraction process is carried out at regular intervals, depending on the requirements of the 
central bank this might be daily or monthly. The timing of the reports can be changed by altering 
the list of overnight reports that is to run each day. Extraction is undertaken by the STRXTRACT 
- rFRAME Interface Extract Report, which runs during phase C of the overnight. This report, and 
the overnight process in general are described fully in the Overnight Reports Guide. 
Information is extracted from the system database grouped into 10 records groups: 
• 
Record type 0 - Exchange Rate 
• 
Record type 1 - Current Accounts 
• 
Record type 2 - Deposit and Loan Accounts 
• 
Record type 3 - Internal Accounts 
• 
Record type 4 - Profit and Loss 
• 
Record type 5 - Bills 
• 
Record type 6 - Investments 
• 
Record type 8 - Facilities and Commitments 
• 
Record type 9 - Foreign Exchange and Interest Rate Contracts 
• 
Record type 10 - Contingent Liability 
 
All internal accounts (general ledger) which are required to be reported on must be defined on the 
General Ledger Statutory Information (GLSRM) screen, detailed in Section 2, General Ledger 
Screens. 
There are two methods of reporting accrued amounts using the rFRAME interface, cumulative and 
non-cumulative. These are controlled by the blueprint parameter BP-STRCUMOPT. This 
parameter can be either: 
• 
"N"- Non Cumulative. Amounts reported by the interface are those accumulated during the 
last reporting period only.  
• 
"Y" - Cumulative. Amounts reported by the interface are cumulative, that is the value sent is 
the total of accrued amounts in all reporting periods.

The following points should be followed when preparing statutory reporting: 
• 
For the correct reporting of period to date information on interest accruals, it is necessary that 
the profit periods are aligned to the periods at which statutory returns will be submitted. Profit 
periods are set up on the Profit Period Dates Maintenance (PPDAT) screen, described in the 
Guide to Setting Up. 
• 
System data should be retained for a sufficient period to allow correct reporting of period 
income and expenses for deleted or matured contracts or accounts.  
  
The following definitions are used by the rFRAME interface when preparing reports:  
• 
Accrual Amount is interpreted as the interest amount accrued to date since the last reporting 
period minus the part of this interest that has been paid or received up to the reporting date 
(i.e. the accrued interest outstanding). 
• 
Interest Payable / Receivable is interpreted as the interest amount accrued to date since the 
last reporting period regardless of how much of it has since been paid or received. Where the 
Cumulative Reporting Option is chosen, this amount will be the cumulative figure covering 
the current and all past profit periods in the current financial year.

currency called the Euro.  
The system supports this conversion process fully for all currencies and all phases of the 
conversion (see "Euro Related Information" in the Core Functions and Inquiries Guide for more

General Ledger Master (GLMAM) 
Before you create general ledger accounts, you must create the general ledger masters. The 
general ledger masters define the ledger categories of contracts and accounts. 
Each master is referenced by a six-digit number and has a shortname and longname used for 
inquiries and reports. You may use the same name for more than one master. 
When you set up the general ledger master table, you must first decide on the structure of the 
general ledger by contract types. Any general ledger account which backs a client account must 
relate to a general ledger master which has a contract type matching the contract type code for 
client accounting (CAAC). Contract types are defined on the General Purpose Narratives 
(GNARR) table, type “CN”, and are not relevant to users of a retail system. 
Note: 
Check your general ledger master settings carefully during system installation. 
Up to 30 related accounts can be defined for each general ledger master. These are used in the 
definition of system generated entries. 
If a specified account is not available when client or general ledger account entries are posted 
through the accounting models, the postings are sent to the real or memo error suspense account 
for the appropriate general ledger master. If the error suspense account for the general ledger 
master is also unavailable, the postings are sent to the system error suspense accounts set up on the 
System Parameters (SPMTR) table.  
You cannot directly delete a general ledger master on the General Ledger Master (GLMAM) 
screen. This action simply causes the general ledger master to become inactive until it is purged 
(after the retention period you have specified). Until it is purged, the master can be reinstated, by 
recalling it for change. The retention period is specified using the retention period parameter 
GLMAM, described in the Guide to Setting Up. Users of the retail system should see  GLMAM in 
the Guide to Setting Up the Retail System.

Setting Up and Maintaining General Ledger 
Accounts 
A general ledger account or a series of general ledger accounts can be set up via two methods: 
• 
By completing the General Ledger Account Definition (GLADM) and General Ledger 
Account Details (GLSTM) screens. In this case, the general ledger accounts are opened 
immediately. 
• 
By completing the GL Account Definition Maintenance (GLADM) screen and setting the 
“Automatic Account Generation” field to Yes on that screen. In this case, a general ledger 
account is opened when a posting is made to it via: 
 - An accounting model 
 - A retail transaction 
 
Note:  
In the case of retail postings, one general ledger account based on a particular general 
ledger account definition must be created by completing both the GL Account Definition 
Maintenance (GLADM) screen and the General Ledger Account Details (GLSTM) 
screen, before automatic generation of general ledger accounts will take place. 
 
 
 A general ledger account is not generated automatically when a posting is made 
directly to it via the CA Backing Account Change (CABAC) screen or one of the batch 
posting screens, such as the Cash Wastes (CASHW) screen. 
When you use the “Automatic Account Generation” field on the General Ledger Account 
Definition (GLADM) screen, you are effectively defining a series of general ledger accounts 
without actually filling the system with unwanted accounts. 
A series of general ledger accounts can be produced immediately by setting the “All Accounting 
Centres” and/or “All Currencies” fields to Yes on the General Ledger Account Details (GLSTM) 
screen. For example, by setting “All Accounting Centres” to Yes, “Account Currency” to GBP 
and “All Currencies” to No, a general ledger account in British pounds will be produced for each 
accounting centre. 
If general ledger accounts have been set up and a change is subsequently made to any details on 
the General Ledger Account Definition (GLADM) screen, you must run the report 
GLACDEFUPD to effect the change across all related general ledger accounts. 
General ledger accounts are closed using the General Ledger Account Close (GLCLS) screen.

Batch Header (BHEAD) 
This screen is used to open a new or existing batch. Each batch must contain postings made in the 
same accounting centre. The number of the batch is assigned automatically, and appears on all 
screens within the batch. 
The postings entered on this screen must have value dates of today or be forward dated. The GL

postings. 
Do not enter the general ledger contra account number for general ledger postings. 
After entering all details, the batch must be closed using the Batch Close (BCLOS) screen. If the 
batch does not balance, it may be closed “unreconciled”. 
Notes: A batch will be closed automatically as unreconciled if the terminal is logged off whilst 
the batch is still open. 
 
 
Unreconciled batches will be purged, by the POSTLST - Batch Postings List report, after 
the expiry of the user defined period. This is defined by the retention period parameter 
BATCH-HIST (see “Retention Parameters” in the Guide to Setting Up). 
 
 
A batch can only be deleted if it is open and unreconciled. If the batch header is deleted, 
all the associated postings are also deleted. 
 
 
Each user may have one batch only open at any time. 
The recommended procedure for reopening an unreconciled closed batch is: 
1. Run POSTLST to identify the unreconciled batch number. 
2. Select the Batch Header screen, enter the batch number and click Inquire. 
3. When the screen is displayed, click Change. 
4. Select the appropriate screen, needed to reconcile the batch. 
5. Either select the specific general ledger account number or scroll through all the postings in 
the batch to identify the incorrect one. This can be changed, or deleted. Alternatively you can 
add a new posting or postings to the batch. 
6. Use the Batch Close screen to close the batch. 
 
Note: 
You cannot use the Batch Header (BHEAD) screen to inquire on, or amend, postings 
entered on the Cash Wastes (CASHW) or GL Bulk Adjustments (GLADJ) screens.

Payment Type Field 
Each payment amount must be identified as being of a certain type (“Payment Type”), using one 
of five options. The amount entered as the “Payment Amount” is transferred according to this 
payment type, as follows: 
• 
Fixed Amount (AM) 
A stated fixed amount (“Payment Amount”) is to be transferred 
• 
Full Balance (FL) 
The whole balance of the account is to be transferred, leave “Payment Amount” blank 
• 
Minimum Balance (MN) 
The amount required to “top up” an account to a stated minimum balance is to be transferred.  
Enter the minimum balance in the “Payment Amount” field 
• 
Maximum Amount (MX) 
The balance in full, up to a stated maximum amount, is to be transferred. Enter the maximum 
value in the “Payment Amount” field 
• 
Above Maximum Balance (OA) 
The amount above a stated maximum balance is to be transferred. Enter the value of the 
maximum balance in the “Payment Amount” field 
 
The numbers 1, 2 and 3 are used to relate payment types with the different payments involved with 
the standing order, as follows: 
1 - first payment 
2 - interim payments 
3 - final payment 
You must enter the first payment amount; if you do not enter amounts 2 and 3 the system assumes 
you wish to make equal payments and uses the first payment amount for the interim and final 
payments. 
Both the payment amount and type can be amended at any time prior to the first payment. Once a 
payment has been made the amount cannot be changed.

Payment and Transfer Type 
With Payment Type “Above Maximum Balance”, Standing Orders can be limited to those that 
involve significant amounts only. This reduces the extent to which transfers of amounts that are 
not fixed are made when the amounts themselves are so small as to limit the usefulness of the 
standing order. The amount of the balance you wish to maintain is entered under “Payment 
Amount”. Any amount above this value is transferred only if it is not less than the 
“Transfer/Minimum Amount”. 
With Payment Type “Minimum Balance” standing orders may be similarly limited to significant 
amounts, or you can define conditions that ensure that accounts are only “topped up” when 
necessary and by minimum transfer amounts. The amount of the balance you wish to maintain is 
entered under “Payment Amount”. If the account balance is below this value a transfer is made to 
the account, in order to make up the balance, subject to the following conditions associated with 
Transfer Type codes: 
1 
The posting takes place only if the amount to be transferred to make up the balance is greater 
than that entered under “Transfer/Minimum Amount”. 
2 
The amount to be transferred is equal to the value entered as the “Transfer/Minimum 
Amount”, irrespective of the actual amount required to make up the balance. 
3 
The amount to be transferred is equal to the actual amount required to make up the balance, 
plus the value entered under “Transfer/Minimum Amount”. 
Transfer Types and Minimum Amounts need not be defined for Payment Types “Fixed Amount”, 
“Full Balance” or “Maximum Amount”.

disallowed for the user who made the Last Add/Update. The Reject operation will remove the

Setting Up Income Statements and Balance Sheets 
Income Statements and Balance Sheets 
The income statements and balance sheets are parameterised reports. The following types of report 
can be produced: 
• 
General Ledger Balance Sheet - GLBSHEET 
• 
General Ledger Trial Balance - GLTBAL 
• 
Average Balance Sheet - AVGBAL 
• 
Income statements (reports Income Statement (1) - STMNTINC and Income Statement - 
INCOMESTMT) 
• 
Statement of Condition - STMNTCON 
 
Each type of report may be set up in up to nine layouts. The formats of these reports are defined 
using the Trial Balance/Balance Sheet (TBBSM) screen. The format parameters can be listed in 
the Income Statement and Balance Sheet Layouts - TBBSLST report. 
The system holds account balances in any number of defined currencies. The General Ledger Trial 
Balance (GLTBAL) report provides output in the currencies of the balances. However, the 
General Ledger Balance Sheet (GLBSHEET) report converts these currencies to the system base 
currency and provides output in this currency by default. There are a number of run-time options 
available with the Balance sheet reports, for a full description of these options and their usage see 
the Core On-Demand Reports Guide. 
Totals on Income Statements and Balance Sheets 
There are four levels of total that can be set up for a report (if a report does not utilise all these 
levels or if a level has a special use, this is indicated in the report description in the Core On-
Demand Reports Guide), The method of totalling amounts is normally as follows:  
• 
Type 0. If a line on the report is not to include any totalling, then set all the Total indicators 
off. This is normally done when you are printing information for a single general ledger 
account or if you are printing a line of text. 
• 
Type 1. If a line on the report is to total all the entries of Type 0 between it and the previous 
Type 1 entry, then set the Total 1 indicator on but set all the other Total indicators off. This is 
normally done when you are grouping general ledger accounts by type (such as miscellaneous 
expense) and want to print totals for that grouping. 
• 
Type 2. If a line on the report is to total all the entries of Type 1 between it and the previous 
Type 2 entry, then set the Total 2 indicator on but set all the other Total indicators off. This is 
normally done when you have used Type 1 as a sub-grouping of general ledger accounts by 
type (such as miscellaneous expense) and want to print totals for a grouping (such as 
expenses).
General Ledger Screens

3937 0457-104 
• 
Type 3. If a line on the report is to total all the entries of Type 2 between it and the previous 
Type 3 entry, then set the Total 3 indicator on but set all the other Total indicators off. This is 
normally done when you have used Types 1 and 2 as sub-groupings of general ledger 
accounts by type (such as miscellaneous expenses and expenses respectively) and want to 
print totals for a higher grouping (such as debits). 
• 
Type 4. If a line on the report is to total all the entries of Type 3 between it and the previous 
Type 4 entry, then set the Total 4 indicator on but set all the other Total indicators off. This is 
normally used to produce a grand total of all the entries on a report.  
 
The above paragraphs explain the general principal of totalling, but the following features are also 
available: 
• 
You can produce a summary style report in which details of the individual general ledger 
accounts are not printed. To add details of a general ledger account (or accounts) into a total 
without printing details of the account, you: 
 
- 
Set up the total line in the normal manner 
 
- 
Set up an entry for the general ledger account using the same line number as the total 
line. Ensure that all the Total indicators are set off for the general ledger account entry.  
• 
You can make a total line print out more than one type of total. For example, if you set up a 
total line with both the Total 1 and Total 2 indicators switched on, then the report will print a 
Type 1 total followed by a Type 2 total. The same rules will apply to the entries included in 
these totals as would apply to two separate total line entries (see above).

The following procedure is recommended for setting up a balance sheet (the same procedure 
applies to an income statement, see the report definition in the Core On-Demand Reports Guide

2. Number each line on the sheet including all titles, unused blank lines, lines with account 
details and totals. Leave gaps in the numbering sequence (this enables you to insert additional 
lines at a later date.) 
3. Select each line that contains a header narrative but no. 
4. List all the account numbers that contribute to each line total. 
5. Decide where you want to print subtotals and totals. On the General Ledger Balance Sheet

sheet; for the General Ledger Trial Balance (GLTBAL) report the equivalent number of 
columns is four. Using the “Total 1” to “Total 4” fields you can choose to:  
 
– 
Print the accumulated total and reset the total to zero 
 
– 
Accumulate the total but not print it 
 
– 
Leave the totals blank for a header narrative line. Blank totals may also be used to  
 
test the layout of a report

Balance Sheet Rule Off Dates (GLROM) 
A balance sheet is usually ruled off after the end of an accounting period when the books are fully 
reconciled. The effect is to prevent any further changes to the balance sheet for the accounting 
period. 
The Balance Sheet Rule Off Dates (GLROM) screen is used to set up the initial balance sheet rule 
off dates and to update the balance sheet rule off date for an accounting period. Postings can only 
be back valued up to and including the balance sheet rule off date currently in use. 
For example, if you want to close the April accounting period, then you set the “Current Rule Off 
Date” field to April 30th. The actual date on which you change the rule off date is at your 
discretion, but it must be after April 30th. As soon as you set the rule off date for the period, no 
more back-valued postings or adjustments will be accepted for that period. 
The original balance sheet rule off dates must be set up using the Balance Sheet Rule Off Dates 
(GLROM) screen before installation has been completed. To achieve this, switch 'on' the  
“Installation Complete” field. 
After adding the initial rule off dates and completing other installation tasks, the Installation 
Complete indicator can be set on the System Parameters (SPMTR) screen (see the Guide to 
Setting Up). Users of the Retail system should see System Parameters (SPMTR) in the Guide to 
Setting Up the Retail System. 
Updating of rule off dates can be done at any time provided the initial rule off dates were set up 
before installation was completed.  
The Balance Sheet Rule Off Dates (GLROM) screen has an inquiry section where the previous 
and current rule off dates are displayed, as well as an update section where the rule off dates can 
be amended. 
If you change the “Previous Rule Off Date”, you must also change the “Current Rule Off Date”. 
If you are only changing the “Current Rule Off Date”, it must be greater than the “Previous Rule 
Off Date”. 
If both dates are being changed: 
• 
The “Previous Rule Off Date” must be set to the “Current Rule Off Date” as shown in the 
inquiry section 
• 
The “Current Rule Off Date” entered must be greater than the “Previous Rule Off Date” 
entered.

Holiday Method 
This comprises two fields. The first identifies the method that 
the system uses to determine the settlement event date, if the 
system generated event date falls on a holiday in the 
countries indicated by the value in the second field.  
The first field indicates one of the following: 
Following (F) 
The system settles the amount on the next available day. 
Modified (M) 
The system settles the amount on the next available day. If this 
falls in the following month, the system will search for the first 
available day prior to the end of the month. 
Previous (P) 
The system settles the amount on the first available previous day. 
None (N) 
The system will settle on the event day, even if it is a holiday. 
The second field contains a value defined on the Country Check 
Codes table (CNCHK) representing the currencies to be checked 
for holidays for each contract event.

About This Guide 
This guide describes how to create and administrate non-retail clients and their accounts for use in 
the Unisys Banking Back-Office Processing product. 
The information contained in this guide is also available as online help. 
Scope 
This guide is for non-retail users and describes the Client functions and associated data screens 
present in the system. Examples of the screens are shown together with information regarding their 
use. Client is divided into Client Administration and Client Accounting. Use of the system from a 
retail perspective is described in a separate manual, the Retail Clients and Accounts Guide 
Administration Guide. 
Audience 
This guide is intended for personnel setting up new clients and their accounts and maintaining 
details for existing client accounts. 
Prerequisites 
Any person using this guide should be familiar with the user documentation. Users of this guide 
should have read the Starter’s Guide that provides instruction in the use of the system. 
How to Use This Guide 
This guide should be used as a reference tool when preparing information for data entry. Use the 
guide in conjunction with a copy of your Guide to Setting Up and your Core Functions and 
Inquiries Guide. Refer to the Core On-Demand Reports Guide for instructions on how to select 
and run the reports that provide this information.
About This Guide 
iv

About Urbis 
The usage of the product name Urbis is due to be phased out as part of the Unisys re-branding 
exercise. The replacement will be the generic term "Banking Back-Office Processing" solution or 
"Banking Back-Office" for short. To provide continuity with existing product documentation, the 
name Urbis is used within this document, but is synonymous with Banking Back-Office 
Processing. 
Organisation 
This guide consists of six sections and three appendices: 
Section 1. Introduction to Client Administration 
This section provides an introduction to Client Administration, briefly describing the relationships 
between the screens included. 
Section 2. Client Administration screens 
This section describes the data entry screens associated with adding a client to the system. An 
example and a short description of each screen is given.  
Section 3. Introduction to Client Accounts 
This section provides an introduction to the Client Accounting module; it briefly describes the 
features available with a client account. 
Section 4. Client Account Screens 
This section describes the data entry screens that are used to set up and maintain client accounts 
on the system. The section also includes the inquiry screens relevant to client accounts. An 
example and a short description of each screen is given. 
Section 5. Automatic Payments 
This section describes the data entry screens that are used to set up and maintain standing orders 
for client accounts. An example and a short description of each screen is given. 
Section 6. Definition of Field Names  
This section provides definitions of all the field names on the screens in this guide. The fields are 
listed alphabetically and details of valid entries are given.
About This Guide

Appendix B. Calculations 
This appendix gives the calculations used by the Client Accounts module. 
Appendix C. Client Account Management Services 
This appendix describes Client Account Management Services functions, including negative

Related Product Information 
Product Overview (3937 0234) 
This document describes the capabilities and benefits of the modules of the Banking Back-Office 
Processing system. It consists of an overview of the system, and a description of each of the 
modules and interfaces available. It is intended for use by senior management. 
Operations Reference Card (3937 0986) 
This document is a single card that provides a list of screen names and their mnemonics. The list is 
organised according to the menu structure of the Graphical User Interface. The card also describes 
how to log on and off the system, enter data, make inquiries and print reports. These instructions 
are relevant to the Graphical User Interface only. 
Starter’s Guide (3937 0531) 
This guide describes how to enter data and make online inquiries. It also includes a description 
and example of commonly used data entry and inquiry screens. This guide is intended for all new 
and inexperienced personnel who need to enter data and make inquiries. 
Guide to Setting Up (3937 0945)  
This guide describes how to set up parameters that govern the operating environment of the 
system. It describes the procedures for setting up the business and operational tables, and setting 
up usercodes and access security. The procedures for setting up blueprint parameters are provided 
with a description of each parameter. It should be used by all persons involved in installation, 
implementation and maintenance of these system parameters. 
Core Functions and Inquiries Guide (3937 0952) 
This guide describes the kernel functions that are used regularly for the maintenance of 
information utilised by a number of modules. It describes the procedures for setting up and 
maintaining data, such as market rates and dealers. It also describes inquiries that are common to 
all contracts. This guide is relevant to all users.  
Settlements Guide (3937 0366) 
This guide describes the processes associated with settlements and customer transfers. It details 
how to administer the settlement queues. This guide also describes how to use the Straight 
Through Processing and Netting functions. It should be used by personnel managing the 
settlements department. 
General Ledger Administration Guide (3937 0457) 
This guide describes the data entry screens associated with General Ledger transactions. This 
should be used by personnel preparing information for data entry.

guide also describes the screens associated with portfolios. The amounts that represent book and

Introduction to Client Administration 
Client Types 
Each client in the system has a Client Type associated with it. All clients of a given type have the 
same basic characteristics. There can be any number of client types in the system, and new types 
can be added on the Client Types Maintenance (CICTM) screen.  
Client types are themselves grouped into Client Categories. There are three basic Client 
Categories: Company, Personal, and Trust. For example two client types Financial Institution and 
Heavy Industry could be classed under the client category Company. This is important, as the 
system will treat the three basic client categories differently, each requiring different screens and 
information fields to be completed. 
Note: "Internal" and "Anonymous" client categories also exist, but these are only relevant to a 
retail system. 
The figure below shows an example grouping of clients. Eight clients are grouped under three 
Client Types, Bank, Building Society, and Industry. The three client types are then grouped into 
the Company client category. Nothing has been shown for the two other client categories, although 
a similar structure could exist for them, depending on your system.

Client Categories 
Client Types defined on the system are classified according to one of the following categories: 
• 
Company 
Business and non-personal clients, for example corporate client, entrepreneur or club. 
• 
Personal 
Any private individual who is a client of your institution, for example staff or a VIP. 
• 
Trust 
A non-personal client holding the account for the benefit of a third party, for example a trust 
fund to benefit a charity. 
Within each category, you may define any number of client types. The category to which a client 
belongs determines the screens you use to set up and maintain client details. 
Client Netting Agreements 
When a client has been created, and their accounts opened, then contracts of various descriptions 
can be made for the client. If a client has many contracts, it is possible to gather these into one 
large payment, so only one payment has to be made. This is termed netting of settlements. There 
are various advantages to using netting of settlements for a client including: 
• 
Reduction in errors and associated operating losses 
• 
Increased productivity 
• 
Reduction in settlement costs 
 
Before netting can be undertaken for a client, a Client Netting Agreement must be negotiated. This 
covers the terms of the agreement, including which currencies and product types the agreement 
covers, and what timeframe it is to be active over. For more information on client netting 
agreements, see Netting of Contracts in the Settlements Guide. 
Euro Related Information 
Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) is a process by which certain countries in the European 
Union are converting their national currencies (also called “in” currencies) into a single European 
currency called the euro.  
The system supports this conversion process fully for all currencies and all phases of the 
conversion (see "Euro Related Information" in the Core Functions and Inquiries Guide for more 
information).

Setting up Client Types 
Client types are identified by a three letter mnemonic. To inquire on the details of the client type 
you must know this mnemonic. Use the Client Type Inquiry (CICTI) screen to find out the 
mnemonic for the client type you want. Now use the Client Type Maintenance (CICTM) screen to 
view the details of a client type. If you are entering a new client type, use the Client Type Inquiry 
(CICTI) screen to ensure that your new mnemonic does not conflict with an existing one. 
Client Types Maintenance (CICTM)  
Use this screen to set up and maintain client types. The client type is a template containing default 
values for information fields that are then transferred to all clients of the type. When adding a new 
client type, the following fields must be completed: 
• 
Client Category.  
This defines the client category the client type belongs to. There are three client categories in 
the system: Personal, Company, and Trust. More information on client type and client 
category is available in Client Types in Section 1 of this guide. 
• 
Description.   
A brief description of the client type for identification purposes. 
 
The following fields contain default information that is added to the client. Any field left blank 
will not be used as a default value on a client. 
• 
Internal Client Type 
The internal client type of the client.  
• 
Industrial Class  
A five digit code used to identify the industry associated with the client. 
• 
Business Group 
The business group of the client.  
• 
Institutional Code 
A code for the industrial type the client is associated with.  
• 
Legal Status Code 
A code relating to the number and access holders of the account have.  
• 
Account Officer 
The account officer assigned to clients of this type. 
• 
STP for Inbound Settlements 
Indicates whether inbound settlements can be subjected to Straight Through Processing 
(STP).  
• 
STP for Outbound Settlements 
Indicates whether outbound settlements can be subjected to Straight Through Processing 
(STP).  
• 
Maximum Amount 
These two fields contain the maximum inbound and outbound STP settlements allowed for 
that client.

Selecting a Client 
The following process allows you to select which client you want to view details for. The client 
must already have been added into your system (see Adding Client Details later in this section). 
The system stores the last client you accessed in memory, and will assume you want to view 
details of that client the next time you open a client information screen. If you want to view a 
different client, you must clear the memory of the old client. To do this select Clear Memory 
from the Common menu. This will also clear other information stored, such as which client 
account you last viewed. 
When there is no record of the last client viewed in the memory, then the system will request that 
you identify the client you want to view by displaying the Client Identification (CACII) screen. 
This is done automatically when you select a client information screen. The client identification 
screens cannot be accessed on their own.   
When you have performed the client and account selection process, details of the client or account 
you selected are displayed on the screen that you initially requested. These details are carried 
forward onto every other inquiry or data entry screen you access that requires the selected item as 
the key identifier.  
Provision of the client selection process gives you a reliable way of distinguishing between 
duplicates and identifying the correct client. To aid selection, the system enables you to use 
several keys to identify a client, for example shortname and city. This caters for the different ways 
that clients may identify themselves to you.

Client Identification (CACII) 
This screen is displayed when you attempt to access a screen for which a client must have been 
selected. 
Six means of client identification are available on this screen. Three of these methods are relevant 
to users of the wholesale system: 
• 
Account Number and Currency 
• 
Client Number 
• 
Client Shortname and City 
To start the client identification process, make an entry in one of the fields. Some of the 
identification fields consist of more than one part, for example ‘Account Number’ and ‘Currency’. 
An entry in the second part enables you to narrow the search criteria; use of this facility is 
optional. 
The first part of the ‘Client Shortname’ field requires entry of part of a client’s shortname only. 
You can enter as little as a single letter in this field. You can enter the client’s city in the adjacent 
field to narrow the search criteria. 
For example if you want to view the details of a client whose shortname begins with THI, you 
select the Client Details - Banking (CIWSL) screen and the Client Identification screen will be 
displayed. On the Client Identification (CACII) screen you enter THI in the Client Name field and 
click OK.

Adding Client Details 
The steps necessary to add a new client to the system are dependant on Client Category. This can 
be Personal, Company, or Trust. Internal and Anonymous client categories also exist but are only 
relevant to a retail system  
There are three different methods of adding a client, all variations on the same theme. The basic 
method of adding a client is shown below. 
• 
Call the Client Details - New Client (CINEW) screen. The only information you can enter on 
this screen is the Client Type. When you have entered this information you will be taken to 
the Client Details – Banking (CIWSL) screen. 
• 
On the Client Details - Banking (CIWSL) screen you must ensure that the new client 
identification details (i.e. shortname and city) do not conflict with a previous client’s details. 
When you have entered this information, you will be transferred to the Client Names and 
Addresses (NAMDM) screen. 
• 
On the Client Names and Addresses screen you can enter up to nine addresses for a client. 
These can either be for reference or to send statements, confirmations and other information 
to. The Confirmation Addresses field on the Client Details - Banking (CIWSL) screen defines 
which of these addresses are used as postal addresses. 
• 
Other screens in the system allow you to enter optional client details. These are not necessary 
for the processing of the client, but may be helpful in recording secondary client details; see

Withholding Tax (CRTXM) 
This screen is used to assign withholding tax rules to a particular client. On any contract that 
attracts interest, for example Money Market deposits, interest can be withheld by the bank. 
This Withholding Tax is payable on contracts when: 
• 
The principal amount is less than a pre-defined maximum amount 
• 
The deposit is to be repaid within a specified number of calendar days from the start date 
• 
The contract matures at call or at short notice 
• 
The client is liable to Withholding Tax (set up on the Client Master) 
 
The amount of tax payable at settlement is always calculated on the basis of the client’s 
Withholding Tax liability at settlement date. Withholding Tax is deducted from the interest on the 
settlement date and is maintained for future payment. Interest rates and amounts are entered and 
reported gross of Withholding Tax. 
Details of Withholding Tax are held on the Withholding Tax (CRTXM) table. You can enter the 
rate and the date from which this rate becomes effective. Note that amendments to the table must 
be forward dated: changes cannot be applied to interest that has already been paid. You can also 
enter the minimum amount on which Withholding Tax is payable, and the minimum time for 
which interest must remain in an account, before it becomes liable to Withholding Tax.

Section 3   
Introduction to Client Accounts 
Counterparty Accounts 
The Client Accounts module processes counterparty accounts that are primarily used for clients 
involved in banking activities associated with low volume, high value transactions. Updates to 
such accounts are effected online and a comprehensive set of inquiries is available to show the 
current position of client accounts. The movement of funds to and from client accounts is also 
reflected in the general ledger immediately. 
General Features of Client Accounts 
Client accounts can: 
• 
Receive postings as a result of: 
- Contract events 
- Batched postings 
- Standing orders 
- Interest settlement events 
- Charges 
• 
Use the accounting models to update the general ledger 
• 
Be the source account for payment of standing orders 
• 
Update the general ledger online 
• 
Reflect positions in the exposure models 
• 
Be declared as a nostro or vostro account 
• 
Post via the S.W.I.F.T. interface 
• 
Back-value postings 
• 
Apply account controls (holds on funds and stops on cheques drawn on an account)  
• 
Provide functionality for Client Account Management Services (CMS), see Appendix C for 
more information. Available functions include: 
- Maintaining account balances using sweeping of funds 
- Analysing the balances, transactions and charges of marked accounts
Introduction to Client Accounts 
3–2 
 
3937 0960-104 
Automatic Payments 
The system provides the facility to process standing orders for client and general ledger accounts. 
The beneficiary of the funds from a standing order can be a client of: 
• 
Your own institution (internal) 
• 
An external bank that is a member of the supported clearing system (domestic) 
• 
An external bank that is not a member of the supported clearing system (foreign) 
 
When a standing order is processed in favour of an external beneficiary, the client’s account is 
debited and an entry placed in a file of clearing credits during overnight processing. There are 
separate files for domestic and foreign accounts. 
You can use standing orders to sweep funds from one account to another.
Introduction to Client Accounts 
3937 0960-104 
 
3–3 
Using a Client Account 
Client Accounts can be set up for banking activities in any currency you use. All client account 
balances are maintained in the currency of the account. For consolidation and reporting purposes, 
amounts are converted to base currency using mid-market rates at run time of financial reports. 
Each client account is linked to a particular accounting centre. You can specify the accounting 
centre when you create the account. If the accounting centre is not specified, the default 
accounting centre for your usercode is used. 
In addition to client accounts, nostro (due from) accounts, vostro (due to) accounts and broker 
accounts can be entered. 
The balance, average balance and turnover for a client account are maintained. The average 
balance figures are calculated during the end-of-day processing. A balance record is created for 
each value date on which there is a change in the balance. Old balance records are kept as part of 
the account history. 
GL Backing Accounts 
Each client account is associated with two General Ledger backing accounts. These determine 
where the account balances will be reported on the General Ledger. 
On the General Ledger master, associated with the backing accounts, one of three contract types 
entered must be “client account”. The codes used to indicate contract types are defined at 
installation. 
Client Account Balances 
Three balances are maintained for each client account: 
• 
Book Balance - the total balance posted to an account, including cheques or drafts in clearing 
and postings which have not yet come to value 
• 
Value Balance - the total balance of an account, excluding all postings that have not come to 
value. The value balance is updated on each value date. Interest is calculated using this 
balance 
• 
Available Balance - the balance available to be withdrawn by the client. This is the cleared 
balance minus any “held funds” 
 
These balances enable a distinction to be made between balances on the posting date and the 
posting value date. Forward valued postings are stored until the value date is reached, then the 
value balance is updated.

reported and used for accrual and statistical purposes: 
• 
Days Credit - this is the total number of days during a profit period where a credit balance 
exists on an account at the close of business. A balance of zero is counted as a credit balance 
for this purpose. 
•

Balance Control Limits 
You can enter up to four balance limits for each account. These limits are held in the same 
currency as the account. The four balance limits are: 
• 
Overdraft Limit - the debit balance limit of the account. After the expiry date has passed, the 
limit becomes zero and any excess is printed on the exception report 
• 
Minimum Balance - the minimum balance of the account 
• 
Maximum Balance - the maximum balance of the account 
• 
Fluctuation - the maximum balance movement allowed on the account from one day's closing 
balance to the next 
 
If overdraft limits are exceeded, details are printed on the CAACOD - Client Account Overdraft 
List report and the CAJOURNAL - Client Account Postings Journal, see the On-Demand Reports 
Guide for details. 
It is possible to apply the overdraft limit to batches of postings entered via the batch posting 
screens, see "Entering Batched Postings" in Section 4, Client Account Screens for further details. 
If a debit posting in the batch will cause the overdraft limit to be exceeded, then it will not be 
possible to close the batch until the overdraft limit is increased. 
Withholding Tax 
Withholding tax affects deposit accounts held by clients liable to this tax. If a client is liable to 
withholding tax, all interest settlement amounts must be paid net of withholding tax.

Account Controls 
The system provides the facility to stop a specific cheque being drawn on an account. Furthermore 
you can hold a specific portion of an account balance to cover a specific transaction or contract. 
Several holds can be placed on each account. 
Interest Conditions 
For each interest bearing account you can define interest conditions. These conditions can apply to 
both debit balances and credit balances. 
Special interest conditions can be set up for a particular account or general interest conditions can 
be set up for a backing general ledger account. Where the interest conditions apply to a general 
ledger category, any account in that category can use the interest conditions specified. 
You can also define an interest condition of “Netted” for an account that has a Related Grouping 
Account. In this case, the system uses the interest conditions set up on the Interest Conditions 
(INTSM) screen for the Related Grouping Account. See “Interest Netting to a Group Account”, 
later in this section, for more details. 
For accounts that have interest condition, you can choose one of two methods for applying 
interest, defined on the Interest Conditions (INTSM) screen. 
• 
Simple. Interest is calculated on the principal on a daily basis. On the defined settlement date, 
the accumulated interest is applied to either the principal account or a specified interest 
settlement account. Subsequent interest calculations are then performed on the new account 
balance and accumulated for settlement at the end of the next settlement period.  
• 
Compound. Interest is calculated and applied to the account on a daily basis.  
 
Interest is accrued at one of two times for each day, defined on the Client Account Static Details 
(WACCM) screen, 
• 
First. Interest is accrued at the end of the first online day during end-of-day processing and 
during every end-of-day until the day you close it; no interest is accrued on the day of closure 
itself 
• 
Last. Interest is accrued during the first beginning-of-day processing after the account is 
opened (at the start of the second day) and during every beginning-of-day after that including 
the last day the account is open

Interest Rates 
Interest rates can be applied in the following three ways: 
• 
As a fixed rate 
• 
As a rate variation added to a base rate 
• 
As a rate variation subtracted from a base rate 
 
Interest rates are always positive and up to 999 base rates are available for each account currency. 
Interest is calculated daily on the value balance. 
Interest Levels 
The interest rate charged or paid on an account can be based on its balance. Up to four interest 
levels can be defined for this purpose. Each level has a maximum amount up to which an interest 
rate or rate variation is applied. 
Interest levels can be applied in two ways: 
• 
On an all-up basis, the interest rate for the level in which the balance falls is applied to the 
whole balance. 
• 
On a slice basis, the interest rate for each level is applied to the part of the balance that falls in 
that level. 
 
A flat rate of interest can also be applied. 
Each interest bearing account can have a minimum and maximum interest rate associated with it. 
If the interest rate on an account is linked to a base rate and the gross interest rate falls below the 
minimum, the minimum rate is used. If it exceeds the maximum, the maximum rate is used. 
Credit account interest conditions are entered gross of withholding tax. 
Interest Settlement 
Interest on client accounts is settled periodically and need not be settled at the end of each profit 
period. For example, interest can be settled quarterly on an account with three months accruals 
included in the settlement figures. The interest settlement posting is created on the day before the 
date specified in the Interest Frequency Settlement field for the client account, and has a value 
date equal to the Interest Settlement Date. If this day falls on a holiday or weekend, interest is 
settled on the next working day. 
Interest can be posted to the same client account or a different account. It can also be held in a 
suspense account for payment or receipt. Postings are made via the accounting models that are set 
up at installation. For more information about the accounting models, see the Guide to Setting Up. 
You can post a net interest settlement amount if credit and debit interest settlement is made to an 
account on the same day and the settlement frequencies are the same.

You can also enter a “Guaranteed Amount” on the Interest Conditions (INTSM) screen. In the 
event of credit interest this will be the minimum interest payable to the client. For debit interest 
this will be the maximum interest chargeable to the client. 
For clients liable to withholding tax, this is calculated on the actual interest settled to an account. 
Therefore, if a client has minimum guaranteed interest and the calculated accrual is less than this, 
the minimum guaranteed interest amount is settled and withholding tax is calculated on this 
amount. 
Interest rates and settlement amounts are reported gross of withholding tax. 
For foreign currency accounts the withholding tax amount is converted to base currency using the 
mid-market exchange rate. 
Interest Netting to a Group Account 
If you maintain more than one account for a single client, you can group accounts together and 
settle total credit interest and total debit interest into a separate account for that group. Interest is 
applied on the accumulated debit balance and the accumulated credit balance of the group as 
opposed to each group member. 
The group account is called the “Group Account for Interest Netting”. The accounts that have 
interest settled into a group account for interest netting are called “netted” accounts. The interest 
condition for these accounts is “netted”. 
Note: Postings to netted accounts are made during the normal business day and duplicate 
postings to the group accounts are made during the overnight process. Interest is calculated on 
the balance in the group accounts and is then settled to the settlement account. 
How Interest Conditions are Applied 
Interest is only calculated on the accumulated debit balance and the accumulated credit balance of 
the Group Account for Interest Netting. Since netted accounts cannot accrue interest separately 
they do not require separate interest conditions to be set up for them. 
The interest conditions for interest netting accounts are set up on the Interest Conditions (INTSM) 
screen. 
When you change interest conditions for Real accounts from Special or General to Netted: 
• 
The change is only effective from the date of amendment  
• 
An interest settlement to settle all outstanding debit or credit interest on the account is 
automatically generated for the date of the amendment 
 
If an account has netted interest conditions attached to it you can only change these conditions by 
closing the account and opening a new one. 
All postings made to netted accounts are duplicated for the Related Grouping Account.

Back-valued postings for a netted account must have a value date equal to or greater than the date 
on which netted interest conditions were specified for it. If the back-valued date is before this date 
for a manual posting an error message is displayed; if the back-valued date is before this date for 
an automatic posting, then the date on which netted interest conditions were specified for the 
account is used as the value date. 
How to Set Netted Interest Conditions for Groups of Accounts 
To set up netted interest conditions for client accounts: 
1. Set up backing general ledger accounts using the GL Account Definition Maintenance 
(GLADM) and General Ledger Account Details (GLSTM) screens, or change an existing 
backing general ledger account using the CA Backing Account Change (CABAC) screen. For 
a netted account these must be real accounts, but for interest netting accounts they must be 
memo accounts 
2. Set up Interest Conditions for the Group Account for Interest Netting on the Interest 
Conditions (INTSM) screen 
3. Create a Group Account for Interest Netting on the Client Account Maintenance (CAHDR) 
and Client Account Static Details (WACCM) screens 
4. Create the client accounts, specifying: 
− The Group Account for Interest Netting 
− The interest conditions (Netted) for the credit and debit account

Cost of Funds 
Cost of funds is an optional feature, designed for internal use between different accounting centres 
in an institution. It allows an accounting centre to credit/debit an internal funds transfer rate for the 
use of its funds. This functionality allows you to better understand the profitability of each 
accounting centre, taking into account both external and internal transactions. 
One method of charging an internal funds transfer rate is through a Funding Account. Funds are 
posted to the account via the accounting models, from deals entered into by an institution. The 
cost of funds is then charged to the account as interest rates, in a similar way to how interest rates 
are applied to client accounts. The profit or loss associated with a particular product will be 
ascertained by the relevant funding account set up for the product. 
A funding account is defined in the same way as a normal client account. You must first establish 
internal clients, and then create accounts for these clients. The accounts must then be designated as 
funding accounts using the Funding Account field on the Client Account Static Details (WACCM) 
screen, and cost of funds rate defined on interest conditions applied using the Interest Conditions 
(INTSM) screen.  
After funding accounts have been created, they must be linked to the appropriate accounting 
centres and product types, using the Funding Account Maintenance (PRFAM) screen. This screen 
allows you to define in which account the funds for a particular product type and accounting 
centre will be stored. How this is set up will be dependant on your institutions requirements, for 
example, all the funds from one accounting centre could be located in one account, or every 
department could have its own account. The Funding Account Maintenance (PRFAM) screen is 
described in the Guide to Setting Up. 
For a full description of Cost of Funds, refer to the Guide to Setting Up. 
Cost of Funds for Client Account Balances 
The cost of funds functionality within the system can also be applied to calculate the cost of funds 
for client account balances. This does not affect the interest condition set up for the client, who 
will not know about the internal cost of funds settings. The accounting centre in charge of the 
client account will be charged or receive money for the funds used to cover that account. The 
charge is calculated using a Base Rate Number, and an Add on Margin, in the same way as interest 
is applied to client accounts.

Account History 
History records are created both when an account changes and at the end of each period. They are 
retained for a number of days specified at installation and include such information as: 
• 
The interest paid or received each day and withholding tax amounts 
• 
The debit and credit interest conditions which apply to the account 
• 
The base rate for the account and the date of any change to it 
• 
The withholding tax rate 
 
The period history shows the position of the account on the morning of the profit day before any 
postings have been made to the account for that day. It includes any interest accrued on the 
previous night's balance.

Postings to Client Accounts 
Postings can be generated in the following ways: 
• 
From contract transactions 
• 
From interest settlements to client accounts 
• 
Using the CA Backing Account Change (CABAC) screen 
• 
From other systems through Kernel 
• 
Manually entered credits, debits or control postings 
• 
From standing orders 
• 
From charges 
• 
From cashier/official cheques 
• 
Loaded into the system from an outside source as cash wastes  
 
Postings entered manually can be entered in batches or as cash wastes. If entered in batches, they 
must be from the same accounting centre. When a batch has been completed, the expected totals 
must agree with the totals calculated by the system. 
The following types of direct posting can be entered in batches: 
• 
Debit - to debit a client account 
• 
Debit cheque - for cheques drawn on a client account 
• 
Debit control - to reverse incorrect credits to override account blockings and to make interest 
adjustments 
• 
Credit - to credit a client account 
• 
Credit control - to reverse incorrect debits to override account blockings and to make interest 
adjustments 
• 
Paired Transactions - a debit or credit to a client account paired with a balancing payment to a 
contra account. This type of posting is only relevant if you are using the Client Account 
Management Services functions, described in Appendix C of this guide. 
 
Bulk credit and debit postings can be made to client accounts where all postings are cash. These 
postings are batched and need not have the same value date.  
Postings to client accounts can be entered with a value date that is before or after the posting date. 
The value date is the date on which interest, if any, is calculated for the posting. Forward-valued 
postings update the book balance and cleared balance (if not “in clearing”) immediately. The 
value balance available on the account is updated on the value date. 
Postings for client accounts can be made from one accounting centre to another but reversal 
postings must be made at the accounting centre where the posting originated. 
Postings to the backing General Ledger accounts reflect the book balances on the client accounts.

If a specified client account is not available when account entries are posted through the 
accounting models, the postings are sent to the real or memo error suspense account for the 
general ledger master associated with that contract, or client. In the case of contracts only, if the 
error suspense account for the GL master is also unavailable, the postings are sent to the system 
error suspense accounts set up on the System Parameters (SPMTR) table.  
Cross-Accounting Centre Postings 
In a multi-accounting centre environment there is a requirement to generate postings between 
accounting centres, for instance when a cash credit is received at one accounting centre for a client 
account held at another accounting centre. 
The cross-accounting centre accounting facility is specified at installation. This enables the 
automatic generation of postings to inter-accounting centre control accounts in the General 
Ledger. 
For example, if a Cash Credit is received at Accounting Centre B for a client account that is 
maintained at Accounting Centre A, the following postings are generated: 
1. DR to contra (cash) account, held at Accounting Centre B 
2. CR to inter-accounting centre control account, held at Accounting Centre B 
3. DR to inter-accounting centre control account, held at Accounting Centre A. 
4. CR to Client Account, held at Accounting Centre A 
5. CR to backing GL account, held at Accounting Centre A, for the client account 
 
A further facility specified at installation enables all cross accounting centre postings to be routed 
through inter-accounting centre control accounts held at the head office accounting centre. In this 
case further postings would be generated as follows: 
6. CR to Accounting Centre A head office control account, held at Head Office 
7. DR to Accounting Centre B head office control account, held at Head Office. 
 
The Head Office inter-accounting centre control accounts for each accounting centre are defined 
on the Accounting Centres Maintenance (ACNTM) screen. The inter-accounting centre control 
accounts for source and destination accounting centres for cross accounting centre postings are 
specified on the Cross Accounting Centre Rules (ACRLM) business table. 
Bulk Loading of Cash Wastes 
The system has the capability of uploading bulk postings created in another system into its 
database. To do this, you must run the report LDBLKPOST - Load Bulk Postings, this will access 
and read the file containing the postings. The postings contained inside will be converted into the 
system format, and entered into the database as cash wastes. The report output contains details of 
the postings converted, and any postings that could not be converted.

Back-valued Postings to Client Accounts 
A posting made in the current period with a value date earlier than the as-of date is referred to as a 
back-valued posting. An interest condition change or a base rate change may cause back-valued 
postings to be made. Interest may be recalculated from the value date of the back-valued posting 
to the as-of date. The history details and account balances are also updated. 
Note: Back-valued postings before an interest settlement event may result in interest earned being 
different from that earned on the back-value date. This is because the interest settled would have 
been different, and if capitalised on the account would have changed the subsequent daily 
accrual figure. To compensate for the loss of interest that would have been earned from the latest 
settlement date if the back-valued posting had been made on time, a manual adjustment must be 
posted. 
Pre-history Postings 
Postings to client accounts that are entered with a value date prior to the current retention date are 
known as “pre-history postings”. 
When entering a pre-history posting you should enter a manual interest adjustment figure to reflect 
interest accrual between the posting value date and the current retention date. The interest 
adjustment figure for the period between the retention period and the system as-of date is 
calculated by the system. The following diagram represents this: 
 
Note: If the Retention Date precedes the “earliest history date” a warning message is printed, 
informing you that an extra interest adjustment calculation may be required to cover interest 
accrual between the retention date and the earliest history date. 
You can only reverse a pre-history posting which was originally entered as such, not one which 
has merely slipped beyond the retention date. 
Hold Funds 
Funds can be held on a client account to cover, for example, a cheque or payment on a contract. 
When the associated transaction or contract has been processed, the hold is cancelled. Any 
number of holds can be placed on each account.

Stopped Cheques 
You can stop either a single cheque or a range of cheques. When a cheque is stopped, any attempt 
to debit the cheque is rejected. Once a cheque has been presented, it cannot be stopped. 
Client Account Statements 
Interim and non-interim statements are produced. The format of statements is defined at 
installation. See the Core On-Demand Reports Guide for further details of statements. 
Interim statements are produced on demand. Non-interim statements are produced at intervals 
specified for each account. Up to 9 copies of each statement can be produced for up to 9 client 
addresses. 
Interest Statements 
Client interest statements are produced either automatically or on demand. These list the interest 
payments and charges for each account over specified accounting periods, and show how interest 
is calculated. 
Account Charges 
Account Charge conditions can be specific to a single account or to a group of accounts within a 
accounting centre. Using the Client Account Static Details (WACCM) screen you can specify 
whether or not a client account is liable to charges. The frequency and scale of such charges 
depends on the account type and usage. 
For client batch postings entered using the Paired Client Account Transaction Maintenance 
(CATRM) screen, different charge conditions apply. These are called Immediate Charges and are 
described in Appendix C, Client Account Management Services.

Standing Orders 
You can use standing orders to automate payments to and from client accounts. The beneficiary of 
an automatic payment can be another account held within the system or an external beneficiary. 
Payment Dates and Amounts 
When setting up a standing order a first payment date and a final payment date, together with a 
frequency trigger, can be specified for interim payments. The transfer amounts can be either fixed 
or variable. Variable transfer amounts can be used to sweep the full balance (this can be capped) 
or a portion of the balance that is over a specified amount to another account. You can also 
transfer the amount that is required to bring the balance of another account up to a specified 
amount. The first and last payment amounts can be different to the interim payment amounts. The 
final transfer amount can be open-ended and the final payment date can either be changed or left 
blank. If it is left blank the standing order events occur at profit period end. 
Cross-Currency Transfers 
Standing orders can be single or cross-currency transfers. The exchange rate (counter, mid-market 
or market) to be used for a cross-currency transfer is specified when the standing order is set up 
and can be amended at any time prior to the payment date. 
Multiple Transfers Using Standing Orders  
You can specify all accounting centres and/or all currencies for a single standing order. This 
enables transfers on either a “many to one” or a “many to many” basis, and so avoids the need for 
repetitive data entry.

The accounts between which payments are made are automatically identified, on the basis of the 
nostros and agents that have been set up for each particular contract giving rise to the notice or 
payment. Default nostro and agents may be allocated according to rules set up on the Nostro 
Settlement Defaults (NSDFM) and the Agent Settlement Defaults (AGDFM) tables. If 
compensating payments are being made through a Nostro, the payments can be netted so that no 
actual payment is made. 
A nostro account is defined as “our account with another bank” (the correspondent). In order to 
correctly reflect any money held with another bank, a copy of the nostro account is maintained in 
its own books. 
Nostro accounts are set up using the Nostro Details (NSTRO) table. They are identified by a 
nostro number and currency or a nostro name and currency. 
An agent is defined as a “third party responsible for paying or receiving funds on a contract”. 
Agents are set up using the Agent Details (AGNTM) table. They are identified by an agent 
nickname. 
For details of how to set up nostros and agents, see the Settlements Guide. 
Nostros and Agents are specified when entering certain contracts under the Client Accounting 
module. In order that instructions for the transfer of funds are correctly generated (using either the 
S.W.I.F.T. network, if applicable, or printed messages), the system ensures that only valid 
combinations of nostros and agents can be specified for each contract.

Net Settlement of Interest 
For an account that has the same credit and debit interest settlement frequencies, credit and debit 
interest are settled on the same day. This interest may be netted and settled by one posting to the 
account. 
To post a net interest settlement amount to an account, complete the following steps: 
1. Set up the accounting models for Net Interest (NI). Refer to “Setting Up Accounting Models” 
in the Guide to Setting Up. 
2. Specify the account, for which interest is to be settled as a net amount, by switching on the 
Net Settlement indicator. 
3. Ensure that the interest settlement frequency is the same for both debit and credit interest 
settlement. 
 
How to Create a Group Account for Interest Netting 
Group accounts are used to calculate interest based on the overall balance of multiple accounts for 
a single client. They are created and maintained using the Client Account Maintenance (CAHDR) 
and Client Account Static Details (WACCM) screens. 
To set up a group account for interest netting, the following conditions must be specified on the 
Client Account Maintenance (CAHDR) screen: 
• 
‘Account Type’ must be set to Group 
• 
‘Group Account Number for Interest Netting’ should be specified 
 
The following conditions must be specified on the Client Account Static Details (WACCM) 
screen: 
• 
Interest Conditions (credit and debit) can be General or Special but not Netted 
• 
Account status must be ‘Active’ 
• 
Backing general ledger accounts (credit and debit) must be memo accounts 
 
A Group Account for interest netting can only be closed when all the netted accounts relating to it 
have been closed.

How to Create a Netted Account 
The Client Account Maintenance (CAHDR) and Client Account Static Details (WACCM) screens 
are used to create and maintain netted accounts. These belong to an account group and contribute 
to the balance of a related grouping account, for the purpose of interest calculation. 
To set up a netted account, the following conditions must be specified on the Client Account 
Maintenance (CAHDR) screen: 
•

•

•

•

Details (WACCM) screen must be Netted.
